title: 6 months of vibe coding and I made this... what do you think?
author: potateo2
selftext:
My goal is to build an educational game/curriculum that has financial literacy education baked into the gameplay loop. I think AI offers a lot to non-technical individuals to just prototype an idea, and so I thought I'd try my hand at building something with AI that potentially is beneficial to some users, and after some feedback, beneficial to even more users. 

I am about as big of a noob as you can get to game dev, but I've been at it for over 6 months now so I feel like I have gotten somewhere. Definitely a lot of things that can be improved and use some touching up (animations/consistency in graphics for one), but for an MVP, I think it gets the point across. That's my opinion, but I'm posting here to hear yours hahaha. What can I improve on? What's the general idea? Is it good to launch with? Is it decent for an AI game? Will this get destroyed if I launch on itch or steam or product hunt?

On another note, here are some questions I had. What is a good stack for designing sprites/UI/UX/animations with AI? Just Nano Banana? Is there anything out there that is great at helping with the art side of gaming?

If you need to see more than just the video to provide some feedback, please visit [fortunevalley.alorafinance.com](http://fortunevalley.alorafinance.com)

All feedback is helpful. Thanks!

comments.author: Current_Valuable5646
comments.body: Could you tell us what are 3 most difficult things you've encountered when doing vibe code? Also the game looks good to me

replies.author: potateo2
replies.body:
Thanks for the support! So I really started not knowing anything about the game engine, coding, or game dev as a whole. So to put my answers in perspective I thought that’d be beneficial. But here’s my answers

1. Getting familiar with the Unite Editor UI/UX. As simple as it sounds, not knowing how to maneuver around the editor and having to look everything up was brutal. Took the motivation out of me seeing how slowly I was moving. 
2. Not knowing how systems worked within the game. Telling AI your end goal is utterly useless if you do not provide information on how to get there. If what you want is anything more complex than a player movement system, you’ll be debugging for hours and end up with 30 scripts for a 2 script job. Watch a YouTube video on whatever you want built. Think of it from a system POV and detail that to the AI in the context of your project. Use real variable/function names. Be as specific as possible and always allow AI to ask any follow up questions if it is unsure on its goal/how to get there. 
3. Knowing how to prompt. XML was a blessing for me. Learning how to generate a good, detailed, and organized prompt was awesome. I built a custom GPT with my project instructions to help with prompting and it worked wonders. Helped me reduce debugging by a considerable amount. 

At the end of the day I am very new to this. Take this all with a grain of salt. I am not a technical individual, so I think whatever I say may not be as beneficial as someone who knows what they’re talking about. But I hope this helps at least a little bit. Good luck!

replies.author: Many-Ad6137
replies.body: How do you make your own gpt? Sounds useful!

replies.author: potateo2
replies.body:
I think it's called project now, but the idea still applies. I use ChatGPT, and create a project. In this project, I can add specific instructions that tell the AI how to respond to whatever I send in chats inside that project.

I used normal ChatGPT to generate those instructions for me in XML format. Just told it my end goal, what I was doing, some rules, more context, the requirement for the AI to always respond with questions if it is unsure or unclear on an instruction I provided, etc.. From there you get much better & quicker responses.

comments.author: LimeBlossom_TTV
comments.body: I've been a game dev for a few years.  I think one of the issues you'll run into is the diversity of your gameplay.  You should scope down so that you can get quality feedback and iteration done on the core gameplay loop.  It takes a long time to iterate on game design, even for a paper prototype, so the more you're trying to design at once the harder it is.

replies.author: potateo2
replies.body:
This is awesome. Thank you for the thoughtful advice. I appreciate it. 

When you say scope down, what do you mean? Right now I have 5 mini games, a home base scene, a job scene, shop scene, and accidents scene. Is that too much? Go even smaller from there? 

I would love to hear back from some users on how/where to improve, but I am unsure where to even get players on the game. Would you happen to know any resources when it comes to that? 

But I will keep iterations from users at the front of my mind so I don’t get too carried away developing my personal wishes in the game. Thanks!

replies.author: HaloMathieu
replies.body: Scope down as in focus on one or two features and mechanics at a time to see if the gameplay loop is fun and flows smoothly. Do you need an character to walk around a town if its just mini-games that you play? Can cut down to just using Menu UIs to navigate to the different Mini-games. Also does your target audience want to make burgers then do taxes after? Better to keep things focused and narrow than trying to appeal to a brand audience
